title: Profit, Loss and Discount

steps.title: Cost price and selling price
steps.content: Cost price (CP) is what the seller pays to acquire the item. Selling price (SP) is what the customer pays. Profit occurs when SP > CP. Loss occurs when SP < CP. Always keep these two amounts separate before calculating any percentage.
steps.tip: Write CP and SP first. Only then decide whether the case is profit or loss.

steps.title: Calculate the profit amount
steps.content: Profit is the positive difference SP − CP.
steps.prompt: An item costs ₹800 and sells for ₹920. What is the profit?
hints: Identify which amount the shopkeeper paid and which amount the customer paid.
Profit is selling price minus cost price when SP is larger.

steps.title: Profit and loss percentages use cost price
steps.content: Profit % = (Profit ÷ CP) × 100. Loss % = (Loss ÷ CP) × 100. In standard placement questions, the base for both percentages is the cost price—not the selling price.
steps.formula:
Profit % = ((SP − CP) / CP) × 100
Loss % = ((CP − SP) / CP) × 100
steps.tip: If a question does not specify another base, treat CP as the percentage base.

steps.title: Find the loss percentage
steps.prompt: A phone is bought for ₹1,200 and sold for ₹1,080. What is the loss percentage?
hints: Divide the loss by cost price, not by selling price.

steps.title: Find SP from CP and percentage
steps.content: When CP and profit % are known: SP = CP × (100 + profit%) / 100. For a loss: SP = CP × (100 − loss%) / 100. These formulas reverse the percentage definitions cleanly.
steps.tip: Think of 20% profit as keeping 120% of CP. Think of 20% loss as keeping 80% of CP.

steps.title: Trace a reverse selling-price calculation
steps.content: Placement papers often give SP and a loss or profit percentage and ask for CP. Work backwards carefully.
steps.prompt: An item sold for ₹840 at a 16% loss. What is the cost price?
steps.explanation: A 16% loss means SP is 84% of CP. CP = 840 × 100/84 = ₹1,000.
hints: If loss is 16%, the seller recovers 84% of cost.

steps.title: Marked price and discount
steps.content: Marked price (MP) is the listed price before discount. Discount reduces MP to determine SP. Discount does not change the seller's cost price. Discount % is usually calculated on marked price.
steps.tip: Keep three labels separate: CP (what the seller paid), MP (listed price), SP (customer pays after discount).

steps.title: Solve a successive-discount problem
steps.content: Successive discounts are applied one after another. The second discount acts on the already reduced price.
steps.prompt: Arrange the steps for a 20% then 10% discount on a ₹1,000 marked price.
options: Apply 10% discount to the reduced price
steps.explanation: Begin with MP. Apply the first discount, then apply the second discount to the reduced amount. The combined effect is not a simple 30% off.
hints: The second discount is not calculated on the original marked price.

steps.title: Successive discounts are not additive
steps.prompt: A product marked at ₹1,000 gets successive discounts of 20% and 10%. What is the final selling price?
steps.explanation: After 20%: 800. After further 10% on 800: 720. The total discount is 28%, not 30%.

steps.title: Find the wrong base
steps.content: A student calculates profit percentage using selling price as the base and gets a different answer from the official key.
steps.prompt: CP = ₹500, SP = ₹600. A student computes 600 − 500 = 100 and then 100/600 × 100 ≈ 16.7%. Why is this wrong for a standard profit-% question?
options: Profit percentage should use cost price as the base: 100/500 × 100 = 20%
Selling price cannot exceed cost price
Percentages are never used in profit questions

feedback_by_option.2: There is no rule that profit is always 10%.
feedback_by_option.3: Selling price can and often does exceed cost price when there is profit.
feedback_by_option.4: Percentages are central to profit-and-loss questions.

steps.explanation: Unless the question explicitly asks for profit on selling price, use cost price as the base.
hints: Recall the standard definition of profit percentage.
Check which amount is in the denominator.

learning_objectives: Distinguish cost price, selling price and marked price.
Calculate profit and loss amounts and percentages using cost price as the base.
Reverse a percentage to recover cost price or selling price.
Apply single and successive discounts correctly.
Avoid treating successive discounts as a simple sum.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Profit percent is calculated on selling price.
common_misconceptions.correction: Standard profit percentage uses cost price as the base.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Two successive 10% discounts equal a 20% discount.
common_misconceptions.correction: The second discount applies to the reduced price; the total reduction is 19%.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A discount changes the cost price.
common_misconceptions.correction: A discount reduces the marked price to determine the selling price; the seller's cost price is separate.

common_misconceptions.misconception: If SP and loss % are known, multiply SP by the loss percent to get CP.
common_misconceptions.correction: SP equals (100 − loss%) of CP. Divide SP by that fraction to recover CP.

worked_examples.title: Calculate profit percent
worked_examples.explanation: Use cost price as the base for profit percentage.

worked_examples.title: Find selling price after discount
worked_examples.explanation: Subtract the discount amount from the marked price.

worked_examples.title: Successive discounts
worked_examples.explanation: The second discount is applied to the already reduced price.

worked_examples.title: Recover cost price from loss
worked_examples.explanation: Reverse the percentage carefully instead of adding the loss amount to SP without scaling.

company_applications.practice: Show the percentage base before calculating. Expect reverse CP/SP questions.
Reverse a discount or loss percentage to find the original value under time pressure.
Translate successive discounts into sequential multiplication, not addition.
Mix profit-loss with simple discount in multi-step word problems.
Identify CP, MP and SP labels before choosing a formula.

srs_cards.question: What is the formula for profit percentage?
How do you find SP after a 20% loss?
Why are successive 10% + 10% discounts not equal to 20% off?
srs_cards.answer: The second 10% applies to the already reduced price, so the combined discount is 19%.

srs_cards.question: SP is known and loss % is known. How do you recover CP?

quest.story: A merchant needs to price products without confusing the amount paid, the listed price and the final selling price. Your calculations must use the correct base every time—exactly what service-company aptitude rounds test.
quest.mission: Calculate profit, loss, discounts and reverse selling prices using cost price as the percentage base.
success_criteria: Distinguish CP, SP and marked price.
Calculate profit and loss amounts and percentages.
Use cost price as the percentage base.
